To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a probabilistic classifier can be used to identify transients and variables in the sky, and to direct follow-up requests.
a) we developed a prototype automated classification of transients, and b) the system is now in a stage where it can be tested on real data.
we have developed a methodology for automated probabilistic classification of transient events and that we are currently implementing this methodology on the Pan-STARRS1 survey.
In summary, our research is concerned with

(i) the development of automated, probabilistic, classification of transient events and variables; (ii) the use of Bayesian and Machine Learning methods to classify events; (iii) the automated incorporation of feedback and new information into the classifier; (iv) the automated generation of follow-up requests for specific instruments, based on the classifier output; (v) the development of a prototype event classification tool for the Panoramic Survey Telescope and Rapid Response System (Pan-STARRS) project.
the development and testing of automated methods for the classification of astronomical transients, using a combination of Bayesian classifiers and supervised machine learning techniques.

the development of a methodology for the automated classification of transient events and the automated generation of follow-up requests, based on the results from a large number of surveys, and with the development of an automated classification system, which will be applied to the data of the Pan-STARRS survey.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we are developing a methodology that is a first step towards a system that will automatically classify transients, and that it is a step that is essential for the next generation of synoptic surveys.
the methodology described in the paper is an essential component of any future large-scale transient detection system, and it will be a crucial component for any follow-up system.
the proposed system is a step in the direction of a more effective and efficient use of the available follow-up facilities.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are developing an automated system for classification of transient events, and for directing the follow-up observations of these events to the optimal follow-up facilities.
we are developing a system that will be able to automatically classify the detected transients and variables, and will be able to make optimal follow-up requests.

we are developing a probabilistic classification system for transients and variable stars that can handle a variety of different types of data and can be easily extended to incorporate new types of data and/or new types of events.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of Machine Learning classifiers in this context is a viable and promising approach, and it can be used to improve the efficiency of the classification and follow-up of detected events.
the classification of events is not a one-time task; rather, it is an ongoing, iterative process that is constantly updated as new data are acquired and as feedback from follow-up is incorporated.
the use of Machine Learning techniques in combination with a feedback loop from the follow-up facilities can provide a very efficient and accurate classification of transients.
